topic: TraceBench: Measuring How Tool Design and Agent Instructions Affect Trajectories

key_points: Primary source — TraceBench (Bendinelli, Dox, Holz; ETH Zürich + CSEM; v1 27 Aug 2026). Simulation-based framework generating controlled root-cause attribution tasks.
Root-cause attribution: agent gets time-series observations from a simulated physical dynamical system and must decide whether a system parameter was altered mid-run and which one.

Four clean, controllable task axes: observation noise, domain context (system/measurement descriptions), availability of labeled examples, and submission mode (direct answer vs. programmatic Python script).
Instantiated on three interpretable mechanical systems (BallDrop, BounceBall, MassSlide) so tasks do not require specialized domain expertise.

Results: agents benefit substantially from domain context; they explore data primarily through numerical console output rather than visualizations; they perform worse under programmatic (script-writing) submission than submitting predictions directly.
Benchmark, datasets, agent trajectories, results, and a leaderboard released at tracebench.github.io.
TRAJECT-Bench: trajectory-aware benchmark for evaluating agentic tool use; complements TraceBench by scoring the tool-use process (selection/order/parameters), not just final answers.
Metrics: Exact Match, Inclusion, Tool-Usage, LLM-judge Trajectory-Satisfy; reports failure modes like similar-tool confusion and parameter-blind selection.
Useful as a contrasting 'trajectory measurement' view vs. TraceBench's controlled physical-dynamics attribution.
"The Devil Is in the Interface": controlled experiments on how tool architecture (interface design) shapes coding-agent behavior across six architectures and 11,700 trajectories.
Structured low-level interfaces improve repeat-attempt consistency up to 4.7x vs. a bash-only tool, without changing the underlying model.
Directly supports the 'tool design affects trajectories' theme that TraceBench's review framing centers on.
TRACE: trajectory-based reasoning assessment for tool-augmented agents; scores efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity of reasoning trajectories post-hoc without ground-truth traces.
Complements TraceBench by showing how instruction/agent-design choices change trajectory quality (e.g. efficiency under tool failure).

stats.fact: TraceBench evaluates four LLM agents (gpt-5.5, claude-opus-4.6, gemini-3.1-pro, minimax-m2.7) across controlled conditions on the benchmark.
gpt-5.5 achieves the highest mean accuracy in all six reported accuracy columns; minimax-m2.7 trails by ~46.0 percentage points on average despite similar SWE-Bench Pro scores (56.22% vs 58.6%).

Removing domain context reduced accuracy by 4.2 percentage points for gpt-5.5 and by 6.6 percentage points for gemini-3.1-pro, while increasing total token usage in three of four cases (agents compensate with more analysis).
Agents generally perform worse when required to produce a Python script mapping each sample to a root-cause label (programmatic submission) than when they submit predictions directly.
Agents explore time-series data primarily through numerical console output rather than visualizations.

angles: Tool design is as important as model choice: interface/instruction changes move agent trajectories (echoes 'The Devil Is in the Interface').
Instruction design axis: direct-answer beats programmatic script submission — the 'how you ask' shapes correctness.
Domain context = cheap performance lever: more context lifts accuracy and can even cut token usage.
Trajectory measurement as a first-class evaluation lens vs. final-answer-only benchmarking.
Root-cause attribution over physical time series as a realistic, controlled yardstick for agentic reasoning and tool use.
